name: Character Creation
content:
The characters you create in Renaissance will be stepping into a world that is experiencing a period of change and discovery. Peoples and traditions long isolated are colliding and mixing. Innovation and diversity are omnipresent. Through the choices you make in building your character, you will determine their place in this world by choosing:

  • Their ANCESTRIES, which represent their genetic heritage.

  • Their CULTURES, which represent their lived experience.

  • Their MESTIERE, or adventuring discipline.

  • Their CORE STATS and SKILL RANKS, which represent their natural aptitudes and the skills they have honed in their life up to the point when we are meeting them for the first time.

  • Their initial KEEPING and TREASURE, which represent their current social standing and fortune at the time we meet them.

The countless combinations made possible by these sets of choices are intended as a mechanical reflection of a diverse world. There is no “right” or “wrong” way to build a character.

While certain combinations of choices may be more likely to produce successful dice rolls, know that character advancement is achieved exclusively through failure and overcoming hardship (see Character Advancement).

A character that begins strong may learn and grow at a slower rate, while an initially weak character is more likely to advance quickly. Similarly, as the game progresses, a character who chooses to confront their weaknesses is more likely to learn from them and grow.

To build your character, follow the steps below:

1) CHOOSE YOUR ANCESTRY

The Recent Upheaval (see Campaign Creation) served as a great “stirring of the pot.” As it affected each part of the campaign world, it spurred populations to move into unfamiliar areas. While many places still bear the strong influence of the peoples that founded them, their populations are now richly diverse. As a result, the offspring of these diverse places often draw their heritage from more than one Ancestry.

Your character’s ANCESTRY represents the influence of genetics and anatomy on their capabilities.

Review the Ancestries catalog. Each Ancestry includes a description of physical features, typical ranges for height, weight and lifespan, as well as the Speed stat that the Ancestry imparts to a character. Finally, each Ancestry offers 3 abilities.

You may choose one or two Ancestries for your character.

If you choose a single Ancestry, it means both your character's parents were of the same Ancestry. Their physical features, height, weight and age fall within the ranges dictated by that Ancestry, and their Speed is equal to that Ancestry's Speed, and they automatically get all 3 abilities from that Ancestry.

If you choose two Ancestries, it means each of your character's parents were of a different Ancestry, and their anatomy is subject to the random combinations of genetics. Follow these steps to determine their unique genetic makeup:

  1. Assign each Ancestry heads or tails.

  2. Flip a coin to determine which Ancestry sets their Speed.

  3. Flip a coin three more times to determine which abilities they get from each Ancestry. Pair the first abilities listed for each Ancestry, then the second abilities, then the third. Combine the results into your character's unique combination of three Ancestry abilities.

  4. Set height, weight and age, using the lowest minimum and highest maximum among the two Ancestries as a range for each attribute.

Record all this on your character sheet and, as you do, think about what each element means for your character. Imagine how their anatomy might shape the way they move through and interact with the world around them. If they are of two Ancestries, how does their unique combination of traits express itself? How might that influence their bearing?

Before moving on from this step, you should have a clear picture in your mind of your character's anatomy.

2) CHOOSE YOUR CULTURE(S)

Your character's genetic heritage is the canvas on which their lived experience will be painted. We now turn to thinking about the places and peoples that have shaped their life up to the point when we're meeting them. While some put down roots where they are born, in this world of change, discovery and migration, it’s not uncommon to be born in one place and to come of age in another.

Review the CULTURES catalog. Each Culture offers a variety of images and details to help give you a sense of what that Culture is all about. While most Cultures are best represented in the game as discrete places, some may be more dispersed, depending how your group has chosen to integrate the Culture into your campaign world (see Campaign Creation). Most important for the purposes of creating your character, each Culture offers a number of abilities.

You may choose one or two Cultures for your character.

If you choose one Culture, that means they have spent their whole life so far with a home among that Culture. Choose two abilities from that Culture.

If you choose two Cultures, that means they have spent part of their life with a home among one culture, and part with a home among the other. Whether this represents two discrete periods in their life or a continuous movement between the two is up to you. Choose one Ability from each Culture.

Either way, when considering your choices, think about what part of your character’s life has impressed each benefit upon them. Recall the vision of your character's physical features from the previous step and imagine them moving through the world among these Cultures. How would each Culture influence their bearing, their habits, their dress? What occupations or pursuits might they have been exposed to or involved in? What challenges would they have faced?

Record your Culture(s) and Culture abilities on your character sheet. You may also want to choose a name and pronouns for your character at this point. Examples of common names are provided by each Culture, or you can make up your own.

Before moving on from this step, you should have a clear picture in your mind of your character's appearance, Cultural influences and clothing in the time just before they took up the Questing life.

3) CHOOSE YOUR MESTIERE

Your MESTIERE ("may-stee-AIR-ay" - literally "Mastery" - "Mestieri" is plural, "Mestiere" is singular) is your adventuring discipline: the special set of skills that you bring to the Questing life.

Review the Mestieri catalog. Each Mestiere offers a thematic and mechanical overview of the discipline and a full list of the abilities available to practitioners of that Mestiere, which represent the full range of what that Mestiere will allow your character to do in the game. Some Mestieri also offer unique equipment items. Each Mestiere also defines what it offers to a Novizio ("no-VEE-tzee-oh" - literally "Novice"): an initial set of training, abilities and supplies.

Your character has attained Novizio status within one Mestiere. This is a permanent, one-time decision. It is not possible to switch or combine Mestieri later on.

When you choose a Mestiere, your character gains all of the attributes and abilities listed under its Novizio section:

  • Martial Training: The subtypes and grades of equipment you are trained in using, if any.

  • Engagement Dice/Successes: A set of engagement dice and successes you always have access to, if any. See the Combat section.

  • Base MP: This determines your base MP (Mestieri Points), which are spent for certain abilities. Some Mestieri have a pool of points, others have a base MP of 0 and have methods of accumulating MP throughout gameplay. See the Abilities and Rest & Recovery sections.

  • Abilities: The initial set of abilities you gain for free when you choose the Mestiere. Some Mestieri simply dictate a list of abilities, others may offer some choices.

  • Gratuiti: Supplies and gear that you may always assume you have on hand without tracking it explicitly as discrete equipment items. See the Equipment and Treasure & Keeping sections.

In the app, your martial training, engagement dice/successes and gratuiti are automatically applied to your character sheet when you choose your Mestiere. You'll need to manually set base MP and add abilities to your character sheet.

All of these attributes together define the basic toolkit of the discipline. As your character gains experience through gameplay (in the form of XP), you will have the opportunity to buy additional abilities within your Mestiere of choice. See Character Advancement.

Each Mestiere offers a unique approach to the game. Some express that approach solely through core game mechanics like martial training and abilities. Others introduce mechanics that are entirely unique to that Mestiere: decks of cards with predictive powers, collections of summonable beasts, interactions with the natural environment, systems for tracking spiritual balance, even methods for writing your own spells.

As you consider which Mestiere to choose, recall again your vision of your character as they were before they took up the Questing life. What about their Ancestry and Cultural influences might lead them to pursue a particular Mestiere? How did they attain Novizio status within that Mestiere? Were they driven by desire, necessity or something else? Who or what taught them the basics?

Before moving on from this step, you should have a clear vision of your character at the moment they are stepping into the Questing life: their appearance, their experiences, the purpose with which they are seeking adventure, and the methods and training they have undergone to prepare themselves.

4) DETERMINE INITIAL KEEPING & TREASURE

We now need to determine how we find your character in terms of social standing and fortune. Are they living the high life or down on their luck? Are they on their way up, on their way down or somewhere in between? These factors are represented by their starting KEEPING and TREASURE (see Treasure & Keeping).

Roll a d4 to determine your starting Keeping tier: a result of 1 means Modest, 2 means Comfortable, 3 means Prosperous, 4 means Opulent. To determine your starting Treasure, take your previous roll result and roll a d10 that many times (1d10 for Modest, 2d10 for Comfortable, etc.). The total result is your starting Treasure.

Note that the above method excludes the Wretched Keeping tier as a starting option. If you want your character to begin as Wretched, you may choose to do so, but know that they will be unable to purchase any starting equipment (see the next step) and will not be able to contribute any Treasure to setting their first Quest's Keeping (see the Treasure & Keeping section). It is a perilous choice, but if you feel it is narratively appropriate for your character, it is your choice to make!

Record your starting Keeping and Treasure on your character sheet. Recall your vision of your character and adjust it to account for this new information. Why and how did they attain their current Keeping? What hardships, windfalls, spending habits and/or earned rewards have left them with this amount of Treasure? To what degree are they concerned with their social standing and financial wellbeing, and have these things influenced their decision to take up the Questing life? How do all these things affect their appearance, clothing, bearing and habits?

5) DETERMINE YOUR CORE STATS

Now that you've got a clear image of your character and an understanding of how and why they are taking up the Questing life, it's time to define their strengths and weaknesses in terms of game mechanics. You'll start by rolling to determine core stats, which in term allow you to set skill ranks and calculate virtues, weaknesses and states (see the Core Stats section for a detailed discussion of each of these).

CORE STATS

To determine your character’s initial CORE STATS, roll 5d4 and drop the highest and lowest results.

For example, if you roll 4, 4, 3, 2, 1, you would drop one 4 and the 1, leaving you with 4, 3, 2.

Assign each of the three remaining die results to one of your core stats: BODY, HEART and WITS.

INITIAL SKILL RANKS

For each point assigned to a core stat, add one rank in a skill under that core stat's domain - in the column below it.

For example, a score of 3 in BODY would allow you to add 1 rank each in 3 skills, 2 ranks in 1 skill and 1 rank in another, or 3 ranks in 1 skill - all in the column under BODY.

You will have the opportunity to increase these scores and ranks as your character gains experience (see the Character Advancement section).

VIRTUES

Calculate the base values for each of your virtues:

  • Your base Endurance is 5 times your BODY score.

  • Your base Hope is twice your HEART score.

  • Your base Defense is equal to your WITS score.

Each virtue starts with a current score equal to its base. These base values are recalculated each time the related core ability changes, so you can expect them to increase as your character gains experience (see the Character Advancement section).

WEAKNESSES, STATES & CONDITIONS

All weaknesses - Load, Shadow, Injury - start with a score of 0 by default. All states (Weary, Miserable, Helpless) and Conditions (Insecure, Guilty, Angry, Afraid, Troubled) are unchecked by default.

6) PURCHASE INITIAL EQUIPMENT

Now that you have a full picture of your character's mechanical stats and abilities, it's time to augment those stats and abilities with EQUIPMENT. Some Mestieri may provide one or more equipment items as part of their Novizio, but you will need to purchase any other equipment.

You may spend as much or as little starting Treasure as you like on equipment items before beginning play. For these initial purchases, you may only purchase items from your character's Culture(s). These represent the gear they've accumulated over the course of their life and/or purchased before setting out on the Questing life.

Add the equipment items to your character sheet and subtract their cost from your starting Treasure. Be sure to add any engagement dice and/or engagement successes each item provides to your character sheet. In the app, these are automatically applied as you add equipment to your inventory (note that you need to check the "worn" or "wielded" box for each item you are wearing or wielding for these to appear automatically).

Any unspent Treasure carries forward with your character into the campaign.

7) REVIEW & FINISHING TOUCHES

Review your character sheet and make sure you haven't missed filling out any parts of it. As you review each part of it, think again of your vision of the character you've created. Does each part of the character sheet align with your vision? Is there anything you want to adjust before finalizing? Do you need to adjust your vision based on the decisions you've made?

If you haven't already, fill out the Notes section with information about your character's background, personality, appearance, any important friends, relatives or connections, relationships with various parts of the campaign world, etc. Also think about their motivations: What do they desire? What do they fear? What questions are they seeking answers to?

As you add all this to your notes, it's totally ok - and even good - if you don't have answers to all these questions. Leaving space to discover things about the character is an essential part of bringing a character into the campaign world.

ALTERNATE METHODS

The above method of character creation is a serving suggestion, not a requirement. While it is intended to reinforce the Renaissance themes of diversity and discovery, it does assume you're coming to the character creation process with a blank slate, and "discovering" the character as you go may not be the right approach for everyone, all the time.

If you already have a clear vision for a character and you want complete control over how to represent that vision mechanically in the game, it is totally acceptable to start with that vision and make choices in whatever order you choose. You may hand-pick Ancestry abilities and attributes rather than using the coin flip method, and you may choose one of the following sets of numbers to assign to your Core Abilities: 3|2|2, 3|3|1 or 4|2|1.

With GM approval, you may choose to create a more advanced character. Start by creating a character as normal, then use a budget of additional XP to increase core stats/skill ranks and purchase abilities (see the Character Advancement section). 100 XP represents a character has a few Quests under their belt, while 500 XP represents a seasoned character of great prowess. Work with your GM/group to choose an XP budget within that range. Anything above that range risks leaving no room for the character to grow.

A NOTE ON HUMBLE BEGINNINGS

If you're looking at your character sheet and seeing low numbers, lots of empty ranks, a short list of abilities, a humble set of equipment, you might be thinking, "this is it?" It is. It's by design.

For a new Renaissance character, the world is a dangerous place. A single blow from a fierce foe can lay them flat. A misplaced word in a negotiation can spoil an enterprise. Attacks aimed at a seemingly surmountable threat may go wide repeatedly.

Whatever their worldly origins and experience, all newly created Renaissance characters are united by one fact: they are new to the Questing life. They are going to fail left, right and center and will grow quickly as they make mistakes.

The game is designed this way with these goals in mind for you, the player:

  • You get a chance to explore and understand the contours of your character and their initial capabilities before adding complexity and making choices about how they will grow.

  • You get a chance to rise to the challenge of using a limited set of tools to find creative solutions to challenges, individually and - crucially - together with your companions.

  • Your characters will probably get into some trouble pretty quickly, and trouble makes for fun gameplay.

So, as you watch tumbleweeds roll across the open expanses of your initial character sheet, look at those empty spaces and realize that they represent your character's weaknesses. In Renaissance, weaknesses are just as important as strengths: your character will only grow if they choose to confront them.
